--- title: "Accuracy and speed" --- How closely `stateMINT` tracks `malariasimulation` on runs it never saw in training, and what a prediction costs. ## Held out, not fitted The emulator was trained on a library of `malariasimulation` runs, split by parameter set into 70% training, 15% validation and 15% test. The figures use the **test split only**, taken from the split file that shipped with the trained weights. Every trajectory is a parameter set the model never saw, in any epoch. ::: {#cec5b8ff .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` held-out runs 1,954 time points 306,778 ``` ::: ::: ## Truth against emulator Five held-out runs span the transmission range from the 10th to the 90th percentile of EIR. The dashed white line is `malariasimulation`, the ground truth, and the solid coloured line is the emulator. ::: {#cell-fig-validation .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} panels = sorted(traj["panel"].unique()) fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(panels), figsize=(14.5, 3.1), sharey=True) for ax, p in zip(axes, panels): d = traj[traj["panel"] == p] ax.plot(d["years_from_campaign"], d["emulator"], color="#3987e5", lw=2.6, label="stateMINT", zorder=2) ax.plot(d["years_from_campaign"], d["truth"], color="#ffffff", lw=1.5, ls=(0, (4, 2.6)), label="malariasimulation", zorder=3) ax.axvline(0, color="#8b93a3", ls="--", lw=0.9, alpha=0.6, zorder=1) ax.set_title(f"EIR {d['eir'].iloc[0]:g}", fontsize=9.5) ax.set_xlabel("years from campaign") axes[0].set_ylabel("prevalence") axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="best") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Out-of-sample prevalence trajectories. The dashed white line is the simulator; the solid coloured line is stateMINT. Five held-out parameter sets across the transmission range.](validation_files/figure-html/fig-validation-output-1.png){#fig-validation fig-alt='Five panels of prevalence over time. In each, the emulator\'s solid coloured line lies almost exactly under the simulator\'s dashed white ground-truth line, before and after the campaign.'} ::: ::: The truth is dashed over the top of the emulator, so any disagreement between the two would show as the white line separating from the blue. The two lines stay close across all five panels, and the emulator tracks the pre-campaign equilibrium, the drop when the intervention lands, and the shape of the recovery, including the sharp annual oscillation of a strongly seasonal setting in the right-hand panel. The simulator traces are noisy because an individual-based model produces a stochastic trajectory and the emulator predicts the smooth expectation through it, so part of the residual you see is the simulator's own Monte Carlo noise rather than emulator error. ## Error across the held-out set ::: {#b2065d76 .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
prevalence
Mean absolute error 0.0044
Median absolute error 0.0032
90th percentile of MAE 0.0081
Worst run 0.0568
RMSE 0.0056
Mean bias -0.00037
R² 0.99877
``` ::: ::: These numbers are in prevalence units, so a mean absolute error of **0.0044** means the emulator's prevalence is typically within about **0.4 percentage points** of the simulator's, and a run at 30% prevalence is typically reproduced between roughly 29.6% and 30.4%. The mean bias is about −0.0004, so it is not systematically high or low. ::: {#cell-fig-error-dist .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.2, 3.2)) ax.hist(run_mae["mae"], bins=60, color="#199e70", edgecolor="none") ax.axvline(summary["mae_median"], color="#e66767", lw=1.6, label=f"median {summary['mae_median']:.4f}") ax.axvline(summary["mae_p90"], color="#c98500", lw=1.6, ls="--", label=f"90th pct {summary['mae_p90']:.4f}") ax.set_xlabel("mean absolute error, per held-out run") ax.set_ylabel("runs") ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Distribution of per-run mean absolute error across the held-out split.](validation_files/figure-html/fig-error-dist-output-1.png){#fig-error-dist fig-alt='A histogram of per-run mean absolute error, concentrated near zero with a short right tail.'} ::: ::: The distribution is tight and right-skewed, and the worst single run in the held-out set is off by about 0.057, under six percentage points of prevalence. That error sets the resolution of any scenario comparison, so differences between campaigns smaller than about half a percentage point of prevalence sit inside the emulator's own error and should not be interpreted. ## Speed A `malariasimulation` run of the same 12 simulated years takes minutes, whereas the emulator is a single forward pass. ::: {#66cf78d6 .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
batch size total (ms) per scenario (ms)
1 17.780000 17.780000
8 90.950000 11.370000
32 257.850000 8.060000
128 904.940000 7.070000
512 3254.340000 6.360000
2048 12474.470000 6.090000
``` ::: ::: On CPU, a single isolated call costs more per scenario than a batched one, and most of that difference is fixed dispatch overhead rather than computation. Amortised across a batch, the cost settles at about **6 ms per scenario**, so passing a list to `predict` or `run_scenarios` is markedly cheaper than looping over it, which is why the API takes a list. On a GPU the same forward pass takes roughly **1 ms** (measured on an NVIDIA L40S). For inference at the scale of a scenario grid, the CPU is entirely adequate; the GPU matters when you are sweeping thousands of parameter sets. A campaign comparison that would previously have been a batch job on a cluster can be run inside a loop, or behind a web form, at interactive speed. ## Next - [The models](models.qmd) — what is actually inside the emulator. - [Performance and caching](../05-statemint/performance.qmd) — cold starts, batching, and the GPU extra. - [Comparing campaigns](../06-scenarios/comparing.qmd) — putting the speed to use.
